title: Chapter 27
paragraphs: "If I'd only the heart to give up what's been set in motion... so much trouble wasted... I'd turn my back on the whole thing, sell up, go off like Nikolay Ivanovitch... to hear _La Belle Hélène_," said the landowner, a pleasant smile lighting up his shrewd old face.
"But you don't give it up," said Nikolay Ivanovitch Sviazhsky; "so there must be something in it for you."

"The only thing in it for me is that I live in my own house — neither bought nor rented. Beyond that, one keeps hoping the people will come to their senses. Though it's the other way round — you wouldn't believe the drunkenness, the immorality! They keep cutting up their bits of land and swapping them around. Not a sight of a horse or a cow anywhere. The peasant is dying of hunger, but just try taking him on as a hired hand — he'll do his best to spite you, and then haul you up before the justice of the peace."
"But you go to the justice yourself," Sviazhsky said.

"Lodge complaints? Not for anything in the world! Such talk and such a fuss — you'd be sorry you ever started. Take the works — they pocketed the advance and ran off. What did the justice do? Acquitted them. Nothing keeps them in line but their own village court and their village elder. He'll flog them the old-fashioned way! Take that away and there's nothing left but to throw it all up and run."
Plainly the landowner was teasing Sviazhsky, who, far from taking offense, seemed to be enjoying it.
"But we run our places without anything that extreme," he said, smiling. "Levin and I — and this gentleman."
He indicated the other landowner.
"Yes, the thing's being done at Mihail Petrovitch's — but ask him how. Do you call that a rational system?" said the landowner, obviously rather pleased with the word "rational."

"My system is very simple," said Mihail Petrovitch. "Thank God. My whole management comes down to having the money ready for the autumn taxes, and the peasants come to me — 'Father, master, help us!' Well, they're all one's neighbors; one feels for them. So one fronts them a third, but one says, 'Remember, lads — I have helped you, and you must help me when I need it — whether it's the sowing of the oats, or the haymaking, or the harvest'; and they agree, so much for each taxpayer — though some of them are dishonest, that's true."
Levin, who had long been familiar with these patriarchal arrangements, exchanged a look with Sviazhsky and cut Mihail Petrovitch off, turning back to the gentleman with the gray whiskers.
"Then what do you think?" he asked. "What sort of system should one go with nowadays?"

"Manage the way Mihail Petrovitch does — or rent the land out for half the crop or for cash to the peasants. You can do that — only that's exactly how the general prosperity of the country is being destroyed. Where the land used to yield nine to one with serf labor and proper management, on the half-crop system it yields three to one. Russia has been ruined by the emancipation!"

Sviazhsky looked at Levin with smiling eyes and even made a small ironic gesture at him; but Levin didn't find the landowner's words ridiculous — he understood them better than he understood Sviazhsky. A good deal more of what the gentleman with the gray whiskers said in support of his view that Russia had been ruined by the emancipation struck Levin as quite true, new to him, and impossible to argue against. The landowner was plainly voicing his own thought — something that happens very rarely — and a thought he hadn't arrived at out of a need to exercise an idle mind, but one that had grown up out of the conditions of his life, that he had brooded over in the solitude of his village and considered from every angle.

"The point, you see, is that progress of any kind only happens through the exercise of authority," he said, plainly wanting to show that he was not without culture. "Take the reforms of Peter, of Catherine, of Alexander. Take European history. And progress in agriculture more than anywhere else — the potato, for instance, was introduced among us by force. The wooden plough wasn't always used either. It was probably brought in sometime before the Empire, but it was brought in by force. Now, in our own time, we landowners under serfdom introduced all sorts of improvements: drying machines, threshing machines, the cartage of manure, all the modern implements — we brought all of it in on our own authority, and the peasants opposed it at first, and then ended up imitating us. Now, with the abolition of serfdom, our authority has been taken away; and so our farming, where it had been raised to a high level, is bound to sink back to the most primitive, savage condition. That's how I see it."
"But why? If it's rational, you'll be able to maintain the same system with hired labor," Sviazhsky said.
"We have no power over them. With whom, may I ask, am I going to run the system?"
"There it is — the labor force — the central element of agriculture," Levin thought.
"With laborers."

"The laborers won't work properly, and won't work with good implements. Our laborer can do nothing but get drunk like a pig, and once he's drunk he ruins whatever you give him. He makes the horses sick on too much water, he cuts good harness, he barters the wheel tires for drink, he drops bits of iron into the threshing machine just to break it. He hates the sight of anything that isn't done in his usual way. And that's how the level of farming has dropped everywhere. Lands gone out of cultivation, overgrown with weeds, or carved up among the peasants, and where millions of bushels used to be raised you get a hundred thousand; the wealth of the country has gone down. If the same thing had been done, but with proper care..."
And he went on to lay out his own scheme of emancipation, which, in his view, would have avoided all these drawbacks.
This didn't interest Levin, but when the landowner was done, Levin went back to his earlier point and, turning to Sviazhsky, tried to draw out a serious opinion from him.

"That the standard of farming is dropping, and that under our current relationship to the peasants there is no possibility of running an operation on a rational system that turns a profit — that's perfectly true," he said.

"I don't believe it," Sviazhsky answered, quite seriously. "All I see is that we don't know how to cultivate the land, and that our farming under serfdom was not too advanced, but actually too primitive. We have no machinery, no good stock, no proper supervision; we don't even know how to keep accounts. Ask any landowner — he can't tell you which crop is profitable and which isn't."
"Italian bookkeeping," said the gentleman with the gray whiskers ironically. "You can keep your books however you like, but if they ruin everything for you, there'll be no profit anyway."

"Why do they ruin things? They'll break a poor threshing machine, or your Russian press — but they don't break my steam press. They'll ruin a wretched Russian nag — but give them good dray horses and the dray horses are fine. It's the same all the way around. We have to lift our farming to a higher level."
"Oh, if only one had the means, Nikolay Ivanovitch! It's easy enough for you; but for me, with a son at the university and boys at the high school — how am I going to buy dray horses?"
"That's what the land banks are for."
"So that what I have left can be auctioned off? No, thank you."

"I don't agree that it's necessary or even possible to raise the level of agriculture any further," Levin said. "I throw myself into it, I have means, and I can do nothing. As for the banks — I don't know who they actually help. For my part, anyway, whatever I've spent money on in the way of farming, it's been a loss: livestock — a loss, machinery — a loss."
"That's true enough," the gentleman with the gray whiskers chimed in, positively laughing with satisfaction.

"And I'm not the only one," Levin went on. "I see all the neighboring landowners who are working their land on a rational system; almost without exception they're doing it at a loss. Come, tell us — does your land pay?" Levin asked, and at once he caught in Sviazhsky's eyes that fleeting expression of alarm he had noticed every time he tried to push past the outer chambers of Sviazhsky's mind.

Besides, the question wasn't entirely fair on Levin's part. Madame Sviazhskaya had told him at tea that they had brought in a German bookkeeping expert from Moscow that summer, who, for a fee of five hundred roubles, had gone through the management of their estate and concluded that they were running a loss of just over three thousand roubles. She didn't remember the precise figure, but apparently the German had worked it out to a fraction of a kopeck.
The gray-whiskered landowner smiled at the mention of Sviazhsky's farming profits, plainly aware just how much his neighbor and marshal was likely to be making.
"Possibly it doesn't pay," Sviazhsky answered. "That only proves that either I'm a bad manager, or that I've sunk my capital into raising the rent value of my land."

"Oh, rent!" Levin cried in dismay. "Rent there may be in Europe, where the land has been improved by the labor put into it — but with us all the land is being run down by the labor put into it. In other words they're working it out. So there's no question of rent."
"What do you mean, no rent? It's a law."
"Then we're outside the law; rent doesn't explain anything for us, it just confuses things. No, tell me how there can be a theory of rent —"
"Would you like some junket? Masha, pass us some junket or raspberries." He turned to his wife. "The raspberries are lasting unusually late this year."
And in the most cheerful mood, Sviazhsky got up and walked off, apparently assuming the conversation was over at the very moment Levin felt it was just beginning.

Having lost his sparring partner, Levin went on with the gray-whiskered landowner, trying to convince him that the whole difficulty came from the fact that we don't bother to learn the peculiarities and habits of our laborer; but the landowner, like everyone who thinks independently and in isolation, was slow to absorb anyone else's idea and especially partial to his own. He stuck to his view that the Russian peasant was a swine and liked his swinishness, and that to get him out of it one had to have authority — and there was none — one had to have the stick, and we had become so liberal that we had suddenly replaced the stick that had served us for a thousand years with lawyers and model prisons, where the worthless, stinking peasant was fed good soup and given a fixed allowance of cubic feet of air.
"What makes you think," Levin said, trying to steer back to the question, "that it's impossible to find some relationship to the laborer in which the labor would actually become productive?"
"That could never happen with the Russian peasantry; we have no power over them," the landowner answered.

"How can new conditions be found?" Sviazhsky said. He had eaten some junket and lit a cigarette, and now he came back to the discussion. "Every possible relationship to the labor force has been defined and studied," he said. "The relic of barbarism — the primitive commune with each guaranteeing for all — will disappear on its own; serfdom has been abolished; what's left is free labor, and its forms have been fixed and worked out already, and have to be adopted. Permanent hands, day-laborers, rammers — you can't get outside those forms."
"But Europe is dissatisfied with those forms."
"Dissatisfied, and looking for new ones. And will find them, in all likelihood."
"That's exactly what I was getting at," Levin answered. "Why shouldn't we look for them ourselves?"
"Because that would be like reinventing the way to build a railway. They're already there, already invented."
"But what if they don't fit us? What if they're stupid?" Levin said.
And again he caught the look of alarm in Sviazhsky's eyes.

"Oh, yes — we'll throw our caps over the windmill! We've found the secret Europe was looking for! I've heard it all before; but, forgive me — do you know everything that's been done in Europe on the question of organizing labor?"
"No, very little."

"It's the question absorbing the best minds in Europe right now. The Schulze-Delitsch movement... And then the enormous literature on the labor question — the most liberal Lassalle movement... the Mulhausen experiment? That's a fact by now, as you're no doubt aware."
"I have some idea of it, but only vaguely."
"No, you only say that; you must know about it as well as I do. I'm no professor of sociology, of course, but it interested me, and honestly, if it interests you, you really ought to study it."
"But what conclusion have they reached?"
"Excuse me..."
The two neighbors had stood up, and Sviazhsky, once again heading off Levin's awkward habit of peeking past the outer chambers of his mind, went to see his guests out.
